message.content:
Lions (family *Felidae*, order *Carnivora*) and zebras (family *Equidae*, order *Perissodactyla*) share a very ancient common ancestor – the last common ancestor of the two orders, which belongs to the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**.  
That ancestor was a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly 65–70 million years ago during the late Paleocene, before the lineages that led to modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates split off.

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. We need to answer with the common ancestor. Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga). Both are mammals, but they diverged earlier. The common ancestor would be the last common ancestor of the family Felidae (lion) and Equidae (zebra). That would be an early mammal ancestor. But maybe they want the most recent common ancestor at some taxonomic level. The common ancestor of lions and zebras is likely a common ancestor of all placental mammals, perhaps the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That might be a common ancestor from the order level. The last common ancestor of the two species is probably a common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders. That could be the last common ancestor of the superorder Laurasiatheria. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, insectivorous mammal that lived around 70 million years ago, belonging to the group that gave rise to the Laurasiatherian mammals. Or we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, nocturnal mammal that lived during the Paleocene epoch, about 65-70 million years ago.
